ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
This Source is associated with the 2 April 1808, M 5.7, earthquake, that is the largest event occurred in historical/instrumental time in this portion of the western Alps foothills.
The location and geometry of the source have been inferred using the damage pattern of the associated historical earthquake, constrained by geological data. We propose that the seismogenic source is part of the western termination of the Monferrato-Collina Torinese arc, and is characterised by right-lateral transpressive movement.
The present-day tectonic activity of the western Alps is highlighted by moderate seismicity, and few geological/geomorphological observations of recent deformation. Instrumentally recorded extensional earthquakes are mostly concentrated along the crest of the chain, down to a depth of 15 km, while deeper compressional events occur at the transition with the Po Plain and along the Ivrea body. The extensional events follow two subparallel trends, the Piemontais arc to the east and the Brianconais arc to the west. The epicentral area of the 1808 earthquake falls within the Piemontais arc, close to its northern termination.
The 1808 earthquake occurred at the transition between the extensional and compressional zones, as defined by Delacou et al. 2004. No focal mechanism is available for this event, while Delacou et al. (2004) present 2 focal mechanisms of two small, shallow earthquakes (M max 1.6) occurred near the epicenter of the historical event, both characterised by normal faulting solutions and nodal planes oriented NS to NE-SE. We can interpret this shallow seismicity either as secondary faulting occuring in the extrados of a deeper reverse structure, or as the expression of a truly active extension.
The main shock of the 1808 earthquake was followed by a strong aftershock few hours later, and by another M 5+ earthquake 14 days later (M 5.6, 16 April 1808), which epicenter is located about 6 km east of that of the mainshock.
The two M 5+ earthquakes were felt and produced damages over a wide area, along the western Alps eastern margin, but also across the mountain chain itself. This suggest the probable activation of relatively deep sources.
Due to the low strain rates envisioned by GPS studies, we expect long return times for earthquakes similar to the 1808 event. The historical catalogue reports very few events occuring along the eastern foothills of the western Alps. Low slip rates and long recurrence times, imply that the geological/geomorphological evidence of the seismogenic sources of damaging M 5+ earthquakes are very difficult to detect in this area.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) There exists a fundamental question concerning the geometry and the faulting mechanism of this source, since there are very few geological and seismological data that can be used to constrain these parameters.
2) Another question regards the possible existence of nearby sources, and their geometry and location eastward of this source along the Collina Torinese thrust.
sections.SUMMARIES:
No specific study exists on this Source. Information on the fault mechanism have been derived from papers dealing with regional strain field and active deformation in the western Alps.
Collo (1990)
The author describes lower Pleistocene fluvio-lacustrine deposits, outcropping in the lower Pellice valley, that show probable seismic induced soft sediment deformation. The author points out that this is the first discover of such deformation in recent sediments made in this area, that is close to the epicenter of the 1808 earhquake and is also the most seismically active of the eastern foothills of the western Alps.
Collo (1994)
In this paper the author describes a 2 km-long, NE-SW trending fault, showing evidence of recent activity. The fault, characterized by down to the north dip-slip movement, displaces upper Pleistocene-Holocene morrain deposits and controls the accumulation of landslide deposits.
According to the author the recent age of the fault is suggested by its fresh surface expression, that is in contrast with the fast morphogenetic processes.
Collo (1995)
The author studies Plio-Quaternary faults and folds buried in the plain W-SW of Torino, and defines their structural relationships. On the basis of subsurface geological data he suggests that the thrust fault responsible for the uplift of the Collina Torinese anticline continues southwestward towards the Alps foothill, and that south of it a NNE-trending normal fault system is responsible for the uplift of the Rocca di Cavour and Madonna di Mombruno hills (they are isolated reliefs cropping out in the plain, made of metamorphic bedrock). According to this reconstruction the area near Pinerolo, is were the structures belonging to the northern Apennines interacts with those of the western Alps.
Collo and Giardino (1997)
These workers describes soft sediment deformations in early Pleistocene lacustrine deposits cropping out in the Chisone valley. They also studies at the outcrop scale, reverse and normal faults and small anticlines that deform the deposits. All these structures are related to an E-W directed compression. The authors discard sinsedimentary causes for the deformations and suggests that they may have been produced by local strong earthquakes.
Sue et al. (1999)
They relocate about 1600 instrumental earthquakes and calculate 79 new focal solutions to constrain the orientation of the active stress field in the western Alps. Their analysis shows that the hinge zone of the chain is affected by widespread extension, radially oriented respect to the trend of chain, and bounded along the external zones by a transpressional regime.
They also show that the area in extension is confined to the NW by the former Penninic thrust front, that is reactivated with as a normal fault.
Calais et al. (2002)
The authors use a network of permanent GPS stations covering the western Alps and surrounding areas, to derive the strain distribution and far-field kinematic boundary conditions across the range. Their data show: 1-the occurrence of an E-W (normal to the chain) extension in the central part of the western Alps; and 2-NW-SE to N-S oriented compression in the southern western Alps and Provence. They conclude proposing that the observed strain pattern may result from conterclockwise rotation of the Adriatic microplate, around a pole located in the western Po Plain, near Torino.
Delacou et al. (2004)
These workers reconstruct the present day geodynamics and active tectonics of the western Alps arc, using a synthesis of 389 focal mechanisms, and mapping and interpolating the strain regime along the entire belt. They show that there is a continuous area of extension that follows very closely the crest-line of the chain. They also observe that thrusting is limited near the borders of the Alps, at the mountain front. Both the minimum stress tensor, in the inner extensional zone, and the maximum stress tensor, in the outer transpressional zones, are orogen perpendicular. The workers conclude suggesting that the couple extension/compression is mostly driven by the gravitational collapse of the chain.

pictures.c: Map showing the western continuation of the Collina Torinese thrust, buried in the plain between Torino and Pinerolo (from Collo [1995]). This structure links the uplifted western tip of the Monferrato with the foothills of the western Alps. The activity of the westernmost section of this blind thrust front is testified by the uplift of middle Pleistocene fluvial deposits cropping out ENE of Pinerolo in the "Rilievo di Riva" (marked by an X in figure).

Seismicity and seismotectonic map of the western Alps with focal mechanisms (from Sue et al. [1999]). The epicentral area of the 1808 earthquake falls within the Piemont seismic arc, at the boundary between the cristalline rocks of the Dora Maira complex (DM) and the Quaternary deposits of the Po Plain.
